title: AI-Assisted Attacks Trigger Unauthorized Payments at Indian Banks, CERT-In Warns
excerpt: Attackers altered business records and approval chains to push payments through legitimate systems, CERT-In said — with agentic tools cutting the time from entry to impact from days to hours.
body:
• CERT-In has warned that AI-assisted attackers targeted business records and approval processes — not payment APIs directly — to push unauthorized transactions through legitimate systems at banking and financial services entities.
  • According to the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), attacks on banks, NBFCs and fintech firms led to multi-crore unauthorized transactions through fund disbursement systems and APIs, with money moved to mule accounts and withdrawn via IMPS/NEFT.
  • CERT-In said agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours; it did not disclose how much money was improperly paid out, and the activity has not been attributed to a specific threat actor.
  • For readers: no customer action is announced in the advisory — the warning is aimed at institutions, which CERT-In told to review business applications, critical records, user identities and third-party interfaces.

Attackers are using artificial intelligence to move money out of Indian financial institutions without breaking the payment systems themselves. In an advisory last week, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said threat actors carried out AI-assisted attacks on information and communication technology assets, resulting in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts.

"In the observed incidents, attackers targeted business records and approval processes to carry out unauthorized transactions through otherwise legitimate systems," CERT-In said, in reporting carried by The Hacker News.

How the attacks worked

The methods CERT-In listed are about trust inside the institution, not brute force at its edge: abuse of business applications and service provider-operated workflows rather than direct exploitation of payment APIs; modification of business records or approval relationships, followed by use of legitimate payment processes; use of trusted systems and established approval procedures so transactions cleared without raising an alert; and exploitation of blind spots in independent verification, reconciliation and review of changes to business records.

Separate threat-hunting, CERT-In said, uncovered AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks operating across enterprise, technology, government, academic and research sectors — automating reconnaissance, generating and modifying exploits for known vulnerabilities, running clusters of AI agents in parallel for tasks such as privilege discovery, and modifying scripts and methods when attempts were blocked.

"In the financially motivated campaign against Indian entities, agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours."

— CERT-In, as reported by The Hacker News

The Crafty Falcon campaign

Earlier this month, CERT-In warned that a threat group named Crafty Falcon is behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial firms, using offensive penetration testing tools including ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and CyberStrikeAI. A threat profile by Gurucul, drawing on CERT-In advisories CIAD-2026-0046 (October 9) and CIAD-2026-0058 (November 4, which named the actor as designated by CSIRT-Fin), says the financially motivated actor targets NBFCs, fintech companies, digital lending platforms, payment aggregators and cryptocurrency exchanges, entering through exposed test environments and shared passwords and making small test payments — sometimes about ₹1 — before larger transfers. Its origin remains unknown.

I4C's account, quoted by CERT-In's reporting chain, describes the entry points plainly: perpetrators exploit unpatched software or misconfigured internet-exposed servers, then target automated fund disbursement systems or APIs used for payments and transfers, sending money to mule accounts across different banks to be quickly moved or withdrawn through IMPS/NEFT.

What institutions are being told to do

CERT-In told organizations to review the security of business applications, critical records, user identities and third-party interfaces, and to make monitoring and incident-response arrangements account for misuse of trusted business processes and automated intrusion activity. The Reserve Bank of India has also alerted banks about rising cyber attacks on financial infrastructure and urged them to provide details of their ability to stay ahead of AI-related threats, Reuters reported late last month. What CERT-In has not provided is a total: it did not reveal how much money was improperly paid out in the incidents in its latest advisory, and no specific threat actor has been attributed for that activity.
nri_angle: Diaspora readers banking or remitting through Indian banks and fintechs face no announced customer action, but the advisory explains why institutions are tightening verification and reconciliation checks.
author: Diaspora Desk
